blurb: Silver-grey German gun dog with amber eyes, bred to track, point and retrieve
description: The Weimaraner is a medium to large German hunting dog from the Weimar area, known for its silver-grey coat, amber eyes, speed, stamina and keen nose.
answer: The Weimaraner is a German all-purpose gun dog named after the city of Weimar, recognised as a breed in 1891. It stands about 57–70 cm and weighs roughly 25–40 kg, and is valued for its speed, stamina, nose and courage in the field.

body: Few documented facts about the breed's origins exist, though silver-grey dogs appear in paintings by van Dyck and Oudry. It is believed to come from the Weimar area of Thuringia. From 1879 these dogs were treated as a blue variant of the German Short-haired Pointer, and fourteen were shown in Berlin in 1880.

The Weimaraner was recognised as a separate breed in 1891, a standard followed in 1896 and a breed club in 1897. It nearly died out around the First World War and was rebuilt from a few survivors. The FCI definitively accepted it in 1954.

Males stand some 59–70 cm and weigh 30–40 kg; females are about 57–65 cm and 25–35 kg. The coat may be short or long, in mouse-grey, roe-grey or silver-grey shades, with small white marks on the feet and chest tolerated. The eyes are amber and the ears hang with rounded tips.

The breed is described as an all-round hunting dog with speed, stamina, courage and intelligence. The German breed club states that it belongs in the hands of hunters and needs practical hunting work to keep a balanced nature; in Germany it is not considered suitable as a companion dog.

As a working gun dog used to track, point, flush and retrieve game, the Weimaraner is generally described as needing a lot of activity and purposeful work. In Germany registration requires passing a working trial, and puppies are placed mainly with hunters.

Conditions reported in the breed include cerebellar hypoplasia, hypomyelinogenesis, spinal dysraphism, corneal dystrophy, distichiasis, entropion, generalised demodicosis, refractory corneal ulceration and, in males, Weimaraner neutrophil dysfunction and tricuspid dysplasia. One 2024 UK study found a median lifespan of 12.8 years.

faq.q: Is a Weimaraner a good family pet?
